title: How Seven Bank connected other banks’ cards to convenience stores: from 66 ATMs
description:
Why did a retail group establish a bank in response to customers’ ATM requests? From a provisional-license document scene at Japan’s Financial Services Agency in 2001 and Tokyo’s first 66 machines, follow card connections, partner-bank screens and receipts, branch promotion, remote support and cash management. See how Seven Bank runs an outlet inside a store. Foundation dates rely on near-contemporary company disclosures and its history, not independently obtained regulatory originals. The 2002 and 2005 records, the 2009 survey and 2010 operations retain their separate dates. Anonymous concept illustrations do not reconstruct any particular customer or banknote transaction.

chapters.c19r1t01: Free to you, a bill elsewhere

c19r1h01.text: You want cash from a convenience-store ATM with another bank’s card. This network began with 66 machines.

c19r1h02.text: On April 6, 2001, at Japan’s Financial Services Agency, a person in a suit holds a document beside a table.

c19r1h03.text: The caption says a provisional license was obtained. Yet the bank did not exist.

c19r1h04.text: That stopped me: how far was this document from letting you insert a card?

c19r1h05.text: How could a packet of tissues at a bank branch lead customers to a convenience store?

c19r1h06.text: And was loading more banknotes into a machine always better?

c19r1h07.text: Follow Seven Bank as we trace how a cash outlet in a store corner connects to other banks’ cards.

c19r1h08.text: Once the bank was established, could its machines serve every card?

c19r1o01.text: A provisional license did not mean a working machine. IY Bank was established four days later.

c19r1o02.text: It obtained its banking license on April 25, then began accepting ordinary-deposit account applications on May 7.

c19r1o03.text: The bank opened first. Did the store machines start that same day?

c19r1o04.text: Eight days later, its head office held an ATM launch ceremony. People in the photo stand before a red ribbon, with machines behind them.

c19r1o05.text: Those first 66 machines began operating on May 15 at 59 locations across Tokyo’s 23 wards.

c19r1o06.text: Only then did I see licensing and installing machines as successive jobs within one project.

c19r1o07.text: The company’s first disclosure report starts with customer requests. What else had customers wanted to do in stores?

c19r1o08.text: The group already collected utility bills. Customers then wanted deposits, withdrawals and transfers in stores too.

c19r1o09.text: You could pay bills where you shopped, but that did not let you withdraw with your own card. Financial institutions still had to connect.

c19r1o10.text: Other convenience stores already had banking partnerships in 1999. This group did not invent convenience-store ATMs.

c19r1o11.text: One more machine in a store does not explain a bank’s work. Whose customers would it serve?

c19r1o12.text: The company’s business diagram includes both services for its own depositors and an ATM network for partner financial institutions.

c19r1o15.text: That connection needed an actual partnership. Which bank joined when the machines launched?

c19r1a01.text: Connect the partners, then tell customers. The launch-day chronology also lists the partnership with Sanwa Bank.

c19r1a02.text: In June, the network spread beyond Tokyo. The Shizuoka Bank partnership also brought service to Shizuoka Prefecture.

c19r1a03.text: Locations and partnerships expanded, but new card functions did not all open on one day.

c19r2a30.text: On June 11, the bank also connected its system to the Zengin network. Transfer service still had another step to go.

c19r1a04.text: On June 13, cards from city banks could also make withdrawals here. Did transfers start that day too?

c19r1a05.text: Transfer service did not begin until June 18.

c19r1a06.text: By July 13, there were over 1,000 machines. Installation brought the service to more locations.

c19r1a07.text: As locations expanded, cash in stores meant more than withdrawals. Could stores deposit the day’s takings?

c19r1a25.text: That December, the bank began handling sales-proceeds deposits for Seven-Eleven stores, addressing stores’ needs first.

c19r1a27.text: Machines accepted stores’ deposits. Other people arriving with bank cards still needed to know what they could do here.

c19r1a11.text: The 2002 disclosure report says ATM locations displayed partner-bank signs so customers could identify them.

c19r2a31.text: The company then described the ATMs as shared outposts of partner banks. Whose specifications would their screens follow?

c19r2a32.text: It also described this partnership as outsourcing. Another bank did not have to bring its own machines into the store.

c19r1a12.text: If you had an eligible partner card, the screen displayed information to that partner bank’s specifications.

c19r1a14.text: Services, hours and fees differed by institution. Would the final printed receipt also change with the card?

c19r1a15.text: I had only noticed the cash outlet. I had not expected even the receipt to follow the partner bank’s specifications.

c19r1a16.text: But you only see a receipt after operating the machine. Who tells customers before they approach it?

c19r1a17.text: Stores displayed service leaflets and posters. The bank also promoted ATM uses with the retail group.

c19r1a18.text: That opening packet of tissues was promotional material made by partner financial institutions and distributed at their branches.

c19r1a19.text: The same report also records partners making posters and displaying them in branches to encourage ATM use.

c19r1a20.text: So, in the company’s report, how did usage-count growth differ between newly installed machine cohorts?

c19r1a21.text: The company considered greater awareness after advertising and more partners alongside usage growth in different machine cohorts.

c19r1a22.text: Comparing installation periods, it said the February 2002 cohort showed more pronounced growth in usage counts.

c19r2a33.text: The comparison group was installed in June, early in operations. The company was observing usage growth in different cohorts.

c19r1a23.text: Which cards allowed deposits, and which only withdrawals? The service table lists them separately; your own bank still matters.

c19r1a28.text: Services gathered in stores, but a customer confused by a step could not just ask the casing. Who could help?

c19r1e01.text: There was a way to seek help beside the casing. The 2002 report already records phones attached to ATMs.

c19r1e02.text: When users lifted the receiver, their inquiry reached the monitoring center, which answered operating questions.

c19r1e03.text: You were not asking about shelf products. Whoever answered also needed to handle this machine’s services.

c19r1e04.text: The machine’s phone reached the center. Did deposit and withdrawal data, security and monitoring each take separate paths?

c19r1e05.text: The company linked these four jobs in one managed network, monitored around the clock, with duplicated equipment and lines.

c19r2e30.text: The bank also established a backup center for unexpected events. A store machine had support beyond its connection.

c19r1e06.text: Here I began to see that someone had to keep taking care of a machine. With more services, what about the cash?

c19r1a26.text: The machines served more than individuals. In fiscal 2003, sales-proceeds deposits began extending to businesses generally.

c19r2e31.text: Businesses put money in; individuals took money out. This network would have to manage both sides of cash.

c19r1e07.text: As more machines were installed, what did the bank later change in banknote handling?

c19r1e08.text: In April 2005, installations exceeded 10,000. Second-generation ATMs began rolling out in July.

c19r1e09.text: Looking back, the company says the second generation handled notes faster and held more, improving operation and cash-transport efficiency.

c19r1e11.text: That October, IY Bank became Seven Bank. The company said the new name should make the store service easier to recognize.

c19r1e12.text: You might think more machines, signs and promotion would mean everyone knew whether their card worked.

c19r1e13.text: But a survey of 10,000 people in November 2009 exposed another gap.

c19r1e14.text: The 2010 annual report says some store customers did not use ATMs because they wrongly thought their cards were unsupported or fees were unavoidable.

c19r1e15.text: They misunderstood their card or the fees on the screen. How did the bank plan to close that gap?

c19r1e16.text: A card could be connected, yet its holder might stop short, never intending to take it out.

c19r1e17.text: The bank therefore proposed more visible in-store information and joint communication with partner institutions in its report.

c19r1e18.text: That led me to another question: if some people expected a fee, did every withdrawal really cost one?

c19r1e19.text: If customers saw “no fee,” who paid for connecting their bank and keeping the machine running?

c19r1t01.text: Those bills must be separated. The 2010 annual report’s model leaves customer fees to the bank holding the account.

c19r1t03.text: That bank could set prices or offer discounts under its own strategy. Who paid the machine operator?

c19r1t04.text: Seven Bank received ATM usage fees from partner financial institutions. These two payment flows must stay separate.

c19r1t05.text: Free service for customers does not directly mean no income for the operator. Nor can we guess the fee per transaction.

c19r1t06.text: What interests me is that partner banks became customers too: serving depositors while buying access to this network.

c19r1t07.text: The report compares using the network with building an entire ATM system. Why would partners pay?

c19r1t08.text: Partners could extend services to these locations while reducing the maintenance and funding burden of their own machines.

c19r1t10.text: How many financial institutions had joined this arrangement then?

c19r1t11.text: The model diagram already listed 555 partner financial institutions, not only banks.

c19r1t12.text: They brought different cards, services and prices. The operator was taking on distinct sets of needs.

c19r1t13.text: The annual report has a figure for that. How much revenue did this work generate in that reporting year?

c19r1t14.text: For the year ending March 2010, ATM-related fee income was about 85.3 billion yen.

c19r1t15.text: That was a full year’s revenue for the whole network, before deducting all location, funding and operating expenses.

c19r1t16.text: We cannot use that total as a receipt for one withdrawal, still less call it one machine’s profit.

c19r1t17.text: If someone wanted this network as a backup, who would take over when a problem arose?

c19r1t18.text: The report even lists the network as a backup option for partners’ existing ATM networks.

c19r1t19.text: To earn that reliance, the operator needed more than a connection: someone had to keep looking after it.

c19r1t20.text: You insert a card in a store machine, and transaction messages travel away. What about the banknotes still before you?

c19r1n01.text: The messages first reach relay systems. The 2010 report records two, in Yokohama and Osaka.

c19r1n02.text: ATMs and partner institutions process transactions through them. Both normally operate.

c19r1n03.text: The company says either could handle all transactions if the other stopped. But who watched the machines’ condition?

c19r1n04.text: The same annual report locates support centers in Tokyo and Osaka, on call around the clock.

c19r1n05.text: You hear two pairs of cities because relaying transactions and supporting sites are different jobs.

c19r1n06.text: If a machine has a problem, the center first handles it remotely, coordinating security or maintenance companies when needed.

c19r1n07.text: I had only thought of repairing breakdowns. I missed another pause: could maintenance itself occupy the machine?

c19r1n08.text: The report does list cash shortages, failures, regular checks and even cash loading or replenishment as possible service interruptions.

c19r1n09.text: Then why not just load lots of banknotes at once?

c19r1n10.text: Back to the opening question: more cash can mean fewer refills, but higher funding costs.

c19r1n11.text: Less cash means more frequent refills, pushing up the related outsourcing costs.

c19r1n12.text: You need cash when you arrive. The operator must keep balancing these two costs.

c19r1n13.text: The report therefore records the bank analyzing usage trends machine by machine and managing each according to how it is used.

c19r1n14.text: Beyond analyzing each machine, was there another cash inflow it could manage alongside withdrawal demand?

c19r1n15.text: I had focused on how much cash was replenished. The report turned to nearby stores: they also had money to deposit.

c19r1n16.text: The sales-proceeds deposits introduced earlier had now become part of cash management across the network.

c19r1n17.text: Seven Bank says it enabled nearby convenience stores and other businesses to deposit takings at ATMs, improving cash-management efficiency.

c19r1n18.text: This describes overall management. It does not say a note deposited by one store immediately went to the next customer.

c19r1n19.text: The report then recorded about 1.7 refills per machine per month. Did that mean every location was identical?

c19r1n20.text: It was that year’s network-average operating figure. Different machines’ usage trends still needed individual attention.

c19r1n22.text: By 2010, the machines, partners and management practices kept adjusting as the network’s service scope expanded.

c19r1n23.text: With this network connected, could you walk over now and withdraw using any card in your hand?

c19r1n24.text: You still needed the right card and hours, bank approval, and a working machine with cash. A machine’s presence alone was not enough.

c19r1n25.text: Back to the opening: how did that store-corner machine serve other banks’ customers?

c19r1n27.text: My answer: a retail group established a bank, then linked partnerships, identification, support and cash management into one network.

c19r1ct1.text: Tell me in the comments: which store service did you use before discovering another company was behind it?

c19r1ct2.text: To keep exploring the businesses behind everyday things that handle hassles for you, subscribe to Brand Stories.
